lessonTitle: Work and Energy of Rigid Bodies

blocks.text: A roller released at the top of a ramp reaches the bottom more slowly than a block would, because some of the gravitational energy goes into spinning it. A swinging crane boom and a flywheel starter motor are the same story: energy methods give speeds directly, with no need to find the forces or accelerations.

blocks.markdown: A rigid body in general plane motion has kinetic energy in two parts: the translation of its centre of mass G and the rotation about G. With mass $m$ (kg), centre speed $v_G$ (m/s), moment of inertia $I_G$ about the centre of mass (kg m$^2$) and angular velocity $\omega$ (rad/s):

blocks.caption: For fixed-axis rotation about O, this reduces to $T=\tfrac12I_O\omega^2$ (equivalent by the parallel-axis theorem).

blocks.title: Rolling without slip
blocks.text: If a body of radius $R$ rolls without slipping, $v_G=R\omega$ and the friction force does no work. The kinetic energy becomes $T=\tfrac12mv_G^2\left(1+k^2/R^2\right)$ where $I_G=mk^2$. For a hoop ($k=R$) the rotational part equals the translational part; for a solid cylinder it is half; for a solid sphere it is $\tfrac25$.

blocks.title: Kinetic energy of a rolling cylinder
blocks.prompt: A solid cylinder (mass 12 kg, radius 0.20 m) rolls without slip with its centre moving at 3.0 m/s. Find its total kinetic energy.

steps.text: Angular velocity and inertia: $\omega=3.0/0.20=15$ rad/s, $I_G=\tfrac12(12)(0.20)^2=0.24$ kg m$^2$.

blocks.answer: $T=81$ J, with one third of the energy in rotation (rotational part is half the translational part for a solid cylinder).

blocks.markdown: **Work of forces and torques.** The work done by a force along a displacement is $\int\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf s$. For a torque $M$ (N m) acting on a body that turns through angle $\theta$ (**in radians**), the work is $\int M\,d\theta$, which is $M\Delta\theta$ for a constant torque. Gravity does work $mg\,\Delta h$ on the centre of mass. Work-energy: $T_1+\sum U_{1\to2}=T_2$.

blocks.caption: Reaction forces at a smooth fixed pin do no work because the pin does not move.

blocks.title: Work by a torque on a flywheel
blocks.prompt: A motor torque of 40 N m acts on a flywheel ($I=6$ kg m$^2$) against a constant friction torque of 4 N m for 5 revolutions, starting from rest. Find the final angular velocity.

blocks.markdown: **Pendulum bar.** A uniform bar of length $L$ and mass $m$ pinned at one end O is released from the horizontal. Its centre of mass falls through $L/2$. With $I_O=\tfrac13mL^2$ and the pin doing no work, energy conservation gives its angular velocity at the lowest position.

blocks.title: Bar at the bottom of its swing
blocks.prompt: A uniform bar of length 1.5 m and mass 4 kg is pinned at one end and released from rest in the horizontal position. Find the angular velocity and the tip speed when it hangs vertically.

steps.text: Energy: loss of potential energy of G.
Kinetic energy about the pin, $I_O=\tfrac13(4)(1.5)^2=3.0$ kg m$^2$.

blocks.answer: $\omega=4.43$ rad/s and $v_{\text{tip}}=6.64$ m/s, which exceeds the free-fall speed $\sqrt{2g(1.5)}=5.4$ m/s for the same 1.5 m drop, because the tip of a pinned bar accelerates faster than $g$.

headers: Speed after dropping height $h$ rolling from rest
blocks.caption: Rolling versus sliding from rest.

blocks.title: When to use energy
blocks.text: Use work-energy when forces are conservative or do known work and you want speed as a function of position. It needs no acceleration and eliminates smooth-pin and no-slip friction forces, but it gives no information about those reactions.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Using $\tfrac12mv^2$ alone for a rolling body, using degrees instead of radians in $M\theta$, using $I_G$ with a pinned body instead of $I_O$, and counting the work of static friction in rolling without slip.

points: Kinetic energy of a rigid body is $\tfrac12mv_G^2+\tfrac12I_G\omega^2$; for rolling without slip use $v_G=R\omega$.
A pinned uniform bar released from the horizontal reaches $\omega=\sqrt{3g/L}$ at the bottom.
Work of a torque is $M\Delta\theta$ with $\Delta\theta$ in radians; use $T_1+U=T_2$.

questions.stem: A solid disc of mass $m$ and radius $R$ rolls without slipping with centre speed $v$. What is its total kinetic energy?

distractorRationale.a: This omits the rotational kinetic energy.
distractorRationale.c: This is the kinetic energy of a hoop, not a solid disc.
distractorRationale.d: This is only the rotational part for a disc.

questions.explanation: The translational part is $\tfrac12mv^2$ and the rotational part is $\tfrac12(\tfrac12mR^2)(v/R)^2=\tfrac14mv^2$. Their sum is $\tfrac34mv^2$.

questions.stem: A thin hoop of mass 3 kg rolls without slipping at 2.5 m/s. What is its total kinetic energy?

distractorRationale.b: This is the translational part only.
distractorRationale.c: This is the value for a solid cylinder, $\tfrac34mv^2$.
distractorRationale.d: This adds an extra half, giving $\tfrac32mv^2$, which has no basis for a hoop.

questions.explanation: For a hoop $I_G=mR^2$ so the rotational energy is $\tfrac12mv^2$, equal to the translational part. The total is $mv^2=3(6.25)=18.75$ J.

questions.stem: A solid sphere of mass 2.0 kg rolls without slipping at 5.0 m/s ($I_G=\tfrac25mR^2$). Find its total kinetic energy in J.
questions.explanation: The translational part is $\tfrac12(2)(25)=25$ J and the rotational part is $\tfrac25$ of that, $10$ J. The total is $\tfrac12mv^2(1+\tfrac25)=35$ J.

questions.stem: A uniform bar of length 0.90 m is pinned at one end and released from rest in the horizontal position. Using $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find its angular velocity in rad/s when it passes through the vertical.
questions.explanation: Energy: $mg(L/2)=\tfrac12(\tfrac13mL^2)\omega^2$ so $\omega=\sqrt{3g/L}=\sqrt{3(9.81)/0.90}=5.72$ rad/s. The pin does no work and the mass cancels.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 18 N m acts on a shaft through 12 complete revolutions. Find the work done by the torque in J.
questions.explanation: The angular displacement is $12(2\pi)=75.40$ rad. The work is $M\Delta\theta=18(75.40)=1357$ J.

questions.stem: A uniform bar of length 1.0 m is pinned at one end and released from the horizontal. Using $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, what is the speed of its free end at the lowest position?

distractorRationale.b: This treats the tip as a point mass falling through 1.0 m, $\sqrt{2gL}$.
distractorRationale.c: This is $\sqrt{gL}$, ignoring the factor in $I_O$.
distractorRationale.d: This is the speed of the bar's centre, half the tip speed.

questions.explanation: Energy gives $\omega=\sqrt{3g/L}=5.42$ rad/s, so the tip speed is $\omega L=\sqrt{3gL}=5.43$ m/s. The centre moves at half this speed, $2.71$ m/s.

questions.stem: A constant torque $M$ turns a shaft through an angle $\theta$. Which expression gives the work done by the torque?

distractorRationale.a: The work is only $M\theta$ in joules if the angle is measured in radians.
distractorRationale.b: This has the wrong form; work is torque multiplied by angle.
distractorRationale.c: This would apply to a torque proportional to angle, not a constant torque.

questions.explanation: Work is $\int M\,d\theta$, which is $M\theta$ for constant $M$. The angle must be in radians so that the units are N m $=$ J.

questions.stem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping from rest down an incline, with its centre dropping a vertical height of 1.2 m. Using $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find its centre speed in m/s at that point.
questions.explanation: Energy: $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2(1+\tfrac12)=\tfrac34mv^2$. So $v=\sqrt{4gh/3}=\sqrt{4(9.81)(1.2)/3}=3.96$ m/s. A frictionless sliding block would reach $4.85$ m/s.

questions.stem: Explain why the kinetic energy of a rolling cylinder has both translational and rotational terms. Show that for a solid cylinder rolling without slip, one third of the total kinetic energy is rotational.
markingGuide: Motion is translation of G plus rotation about G: $T=\tfrac12mv_G^2+\tfrac12I_G\omega^2$
questions.explanation: Only the translational part is present for a sliding block. Rolling shares the available gravitational energy between the two parts, so a rolling body is slower than a sliding one.

questions.stem: A uniform bar is pinned at one end and released from the horizontal. Use the work-energy principle to find its angular velocity at the vertical, stating which forces do work, and explain why energy methods are preferable here to the equations of motion for finding speed.
markingGuide: Only gravity does work (pin reaction does none)
Potential energy lost by the centre of mass is $mgL/2$
Energy gives speed as a function of position directly, since the angular acceleration varies with angle and would need integration
questions.explanation: Using $\sum M_O=I_O\alpha$ would give $\alpha(\theta)$ and require an integration over angle. Energy conservation performs that integration automatically.
